title: Five strengths
hook: fourth point: a lifetime's practice in five strengths: intention, familiarity, seed, reproach, aspiration

segments.voice: Yesterday, bad circumstances as the path. Your line was trouble is the path. When something small went wrong, did the line come before the complaint? Day one thousand three hundred.

A toothbrush is a lifetime practice nobody calls spiritual. Twice a day, for decades, mostly without thinking, and it works because it's small and it never stops. Ask how anyone keeps a deep practice going for a whole life, through jobs and moves and grief and boredom, and the honest answer usually isn't a dramatic vow. It's something closer to the toothbrush. Point four of the seven points of mind training gathers a whole life's practice into a short list a person can actually carry. Today, five strengths.
screen: `A TOOTHBRUSH, TWICE A DAY.` → `HOW DO YOU KEEP IT UP FOR LIFE?` → `POINT FOUR: A SHORT LIST.`

segments.voice: First, intention. The strength of resolve: setting the mind, at the start of the day, the week, the year, on the awakened heart. Something like: today, as far as I can, I won't lose sight of others. It's the aim, chosen ahead of time. Second, familiarity. Doing it again and again until it's ordinary. The commentaries on mind training say that whatever the mind gets used to becomes easy. Third, the seed. Sometimes called the white seed: doing good, small and concrete, so the practice has something to grow from. Not big gestures. A kindness, a gift, a held door. Fourth, reproach. This one can sound harsh. It means turning against self-cherishing whenever it shows up, the me-first reflex from yesterday, and saying to it, plainly: you're the troublemaker here. Not shame aimed at yourself. A firm no aimed at a habit. Fifth, aspiration. At the end of the day, a wish, often made with a dedication of whatever good was done: that it go toward the welfare of all beings, and that this training continue. So the day has a shape. Intention in the morning. Familiarity and seed through the day. Reproach when the old reflex flares. Aspiration at night. Tibetan tradition also teaches the same five strengths for the time of dying, so that the practice a person has lived with is the practice they die with. Five words, held lightly, for a whole life.
screen: `INTENTION: AIM IT IN THE MORNING.` · `FAMILIARITY, AND THE SEED OF GOOD.` · `REPROACH: A FIRM NO TO ME FIRST.` · `ASPIRATION: A WISH AT NIGHT.` · then, large: `FIVE STRENGTHS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: set one intention. Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Look ahead at the rest of today, or tomorrow if it's late. Choose one plain intention, in your own words, about how you'll be with other people. Short enough to remember. Say it to yourself once, slowly. Then say it again, so it starts to become familiar. Notice the next spot in your day where it will be tested. Then let it go, and rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Five strengths. Point four: intention, familiarity, seed, reproach and aspiration, a whole life's practice in one short list. Today's word.
Your line: five strengths. Tonight, before sleep, try the fifth: one wish that whatever good you did today goes somewhere useful. Day one thousand three hundred.

howItsDone: Practitioners of Tibetan mind training use the five strengths to frame a day: setting an intention in the morning, practicing and doing good through the day, rejecting self-cherishing when it arises, and making an aspiration and dedication at night.
